rationale.intervention_reconstruction: The hypothesis proposes high-temperature mechanical tests under simulated plasma-facing conditions, while the paper actually performed room-temperature compression, indentation plastometry up to 500 °C, and scratch testing. Both involve mechanical testing of the same alloy versus pure tungsten, but the specific test types and temperature ranges differ substantially.
rationale.condition_agreement: The hypothesis specifies temperatures of 1200–1500 K under controlled atmospheres mimicking irradiation, whereas the paper used room-temperature compression, indentation from RT to 500 °C in air, and room-temperature scratch tests. These are different temperature regimes and environments.
rationale.mechanism_agreement: The hypothesis attributes improved plasticity and toughness to Zr segregation at grain boundaries enhancing cohesion. The paper attributes improvements to Ti, V, and Zr through reduced valence-electron concentration, dislocation-core modification, grain-boundary cohesion, and crack impediment, but does not isolate grain-boundary segregation as the primary mediator. Both invoke grain-boundary cohesion, but the specific pathway (segregation vs. multicomponent effects) differs.
rationale.outcome_agreement: The hypothesis predicts higher plastic strain and toughness at high temperatures. The paper reports higher strength, greater plastic strain, lower BDTT, less scratch damage, and higher fracture toughness, but at lower temperatures (RT–500 °C). The predicted property direction matches, but the temperature context and specific values differ.
